summary: Verified 62 entries: the 61 entries n=1..541 with n mod 9 = 1 (entry 10 is in that set) plus entry 134. Every first page was checked on a first-page image fetched from the Internet Archive scan of OR Ser. I vol. 27 (62 of 62 viewed). Bodies were read from the Archive per-leaf OCR and the historian OCR corpus. Pages and the Dixon marks were checked against the list's own source, the Civil War Cycling OR index (fetched; robots allow). Report numbers, titles, ranks and units match the printed headings in all 62. The list's first page is right in 60 of 62. Entry 10 should start on p. 168 (the list's p. 155 is the first page of No. 9). Entry 298 should start on p. 843 (p. 842 is the last page of No. 297). Entry 134's listed pages 488-492 are right; the historian index start of 486 is wrong, because pp. 486 and 487 are blank plate pages. Description accuracy of the template: 41 accurate, 20 partly-inaccurate, 1 inaccurate (505, a private letter from a quartermaster, not an official after-action report by the commander). Rights: all A1 (US Government work, GPO 1889; the Archive says "In public domain. Work published prior to 1923"). All 62 listed links go to HathiTrust or eHistory and were not fetched (blocked to bots). An Internet Archive deep link to the first page, fetched and viewed, is given for every entry. Verdicts: 60 APPROVE and 2 NEEDS-HUMAN-REVIEW (entries 10 and 298, whose listed locators are wrong; the corrected pages are given).
systemic_findings: Scope and method. 62 items: the 61 entries n=1..541 with n mod 9 = 1 (entry 10 is one of them) plus entry 134. For each I (a) fetched the first-page image from the Internet Archive scan, using the reader index derived from the item's own scandata.xml, and viewed it (62 of 62; the mapping was also confirmed on pages outside the batch), (b) read the body from the Archive's per-leaf OCR and the historian OCR corpus (reports.json, normalized text), and (c) compared pages and the Dixon marks with the Civil War Cycling OR index, the list's own named source (fetched; its robots.txt allows it). Not fetched: eHistory and HathiTrust (blocked to bots), Perseus. Not verified: B. Y. Dixon's book, whether any listed HathiTrust/eHistory link opens the page it names, and any page text beyond the first-page images, which was read from OCR rather than from the page images.

Accuracy of the description template, with the rule used. 'Accurate' means the author commanded the unit during the events (acting commander counts), the paper narrates that unit's part in what the OR prints under 'The Gettysburg Campaign', at least three of the four claimed contents (marches, positions, fighting, losses) are in the text, and the cited pages are right. Result: 41 accurate, 20 partly-inaccurate, 1 inaccurate (505). Causes among the 21 overlap. 11 are not about the unit's part in the battle (a return, the pursuit, a supplement, June operations or a militia tour: 10, 19, 134, 190, 199, 334, 370, 379, 388, 451, 478). 9 are not the full report of the unit's commander (a General-in-Chief's annual summary 1, a signal officer 19, an ordnance officer 316, a quartermaster's private letter 505, supplements 145, 199, 388, a brigade taken on July 4 451, a text copied from a diary 289). 4 hold addenda or other papers under one number (1, 134, 271, 334). 2 cite a wrong first page (10, 298). So about one entry in three of this sample has a materially wrong or misleading element, although the genre claim (an official report by a commander) is right for most.

The template is one sentence reused. 60 of 62 entries carry the identical 'after-action report ... written by the officer in command ... marches, positions, fighting and losses in the Gettysburg Campaign'; entries 10 and 379 use a 'return' variant, and the 'day-by-day itinerary' clause of 379 belongs to No. 426. Ten of the 62 headings are printed 'Reports of ...' (28, 64, 109, 134, 226, 253, 271, 307, 334, 442): several papers under one number, described as a single report. Fourteen of the 62 carry the footnote 'But see revised statement' or 'Embodied in revised statement' (pp. 174-179), so the casualty figures in the text were superseded by later returns and the OCR text alone should not be quoted for casualty totals. The OR's own asterisk notes are these compiler footnotes (for example a medal-of-honor note on p. 281) and the rows of asterisks marking omitted passages (entry 1).

The Dixon asterisk notes. 15 entries in the batch carry them (28, 253, 424, 460 single asterisk; 91, 109, 154, 181, 217, 271, 307, 316, 325, 406, 505 double asterisk). All 15 match the Civil War Cycling index, which says one asterisk marks 'best overall reports' and two mark 'particularly vivid' or 'excellent explanation of events' according to Dixon. Across all 543 OR entries I compared the flags with that index: 0 mismatches. This is verified only to the level of the index; Dixon's book was not consulted, and the list's own preface says the notes follow Dixon 'as reported by Civil War Cycling'.

Page ranges. The list copies the Civil War Cycling index exactly (541 of 543 ranges compared are identical; the three that differ are index typos: No. 9 printed 154-168, entry 471's '74-476', entry 567's '721-'). Against the printed headings, the list's first page is right for 60 of 62. Entry 10: the index itself prints No. 10 as 155-170, but No. 10 begins on p. 168 (p. 155 is No. 9); both listed links point at p. 155. Entry 298: the list says 842, but p. 842 is the last page of No. 297 and No. 298 begins on p. 843. Entry 134: the list (488-492) is right; the historian index (486-492) is wrong because pp. 486-487 are blank plates. An automated heading scan of all 543 OR entries (OCR only, not viewed) found the same start-page error in 10 and 298 and one more, entry 251 (list 722, heading on p. 723, p. 722 is the end of No. 250), and one end-page error, entry 509 (list 654-654, report runs to p. 656). 44 entries had no heading the scan could find (garbled OCR) and were not checked.

Registry and index defects found. The registry's structural check tolerates a one-page difference, which is why entry 298 passed as 'APPROVED-CROSSWALK'; the 32 'differs by one page' notes need a heading check like the one above. The registry's OCR page ranges are stale against the current historian reports.json for 8 entries (11, 12, 72, 73, 227, 228, 462, 463); entry 73's 'differs by one' flag came from the stale value (the heading is at the foot of p. 360, as listed). The historian index still has the wrong start for 134 (486, a blank plate), so its segment begins on an empty page. OCR misreads two printed years, so the index has no date for them: entry 208 ('1868', really 1863) and entry 325 ('I860', really 1863). One OCR number line is lost (397, 'No. 443'), which hides its heading from automated scans.

Dates. The preface calls the reports 'contemporaneous eyewitness accounts ... in the weeks after the battle'. Of the 58 entries with a printed date, 6 predate July 3 (prelude actions: Brandy Station, Winchester, Martinsburg), 9 fall within 7 days after the battle, the median is 25 days after July 3, 24 are 30 or more days later, and the longest is 188 days (entry 370, Jan 7, 1864). Four are undated in print (145, 289, 460; 379 is a strength return). Several authors were not at the battle (134, 190, 199, 388, 451), so 'eyewitness' also overstates.

Gettysburg relevance of the sample (by what the text covers): 31 battle July 1-3, 14 campaign and battle, 11 campaign only (June actions at Brandy Station, Aldie, Winchester, Martinsburg, Carlisle, Harrisburg), 6 aftermath. The OR prints the June actions under the running head 'The Gettysburg Campaign', so the template wording is literally defensible for them, but a reader expecting the July 1-3 fighting would be misled.

Rights. Tier A1 for all 62: US Government publication (OR Ser. I vol. 27, Washington: Government Printing Office, 1889; the Part 1 title page was read on the scan and the Part 2 OCR title page says 1889), 17 U.S.C. 105, and the Internet Archive metadata for warofrebellion271unit and warofrebellion272unit (fetched) states 'In public domain. Work published prior to 1923.' The text source is the Archive scan, not the listed eHistory or HathiTrust pages; the eHistory transcription layer was not assessed. Tables (10, 379) are not quotable from OCR; use the printed page for figures.

Links. All 62 entries link only to HathiTrust (seq = printed page + 20) and, for Union Part 1 entries, eHistory; none was fetched. For entries 10 and 298 the listed links point at the wrong page (No. 9's first page, No. 297's last page). Every entry now has an Internet Archive deep link to its first page (reader index from scandata.xml); all 62 images were fetched (HTTP 200) and viewed, and each shows the heading of the right report.

Extraction hazards seen in this batch: 46 of 62 reports begin mid-page under the end of the previous report and 15 at the top of a page; 21 share their last page with the next report; undated or garbled-date headings (145, 208, 289, 325, 442, 460); OCR-lost number line (397); table-only entries (10, 379); composite entries that need splitting before ingestion (1, 28, 64, 109, 134, 226, 253, 271, 307, 334, 442, 460); supplements that must be read with their parent report (145 with 144, 199 with 198, 298 with 297, 388 with Maffett's).

summary: Batch index 2 (0-based) of qc/review-queue-next.json, i.e. the batches[2] block whose own "batch" field reads 3: entries 605, 606, 608, 609, 611, 613, 614, 617, 618, 622, 623, 627 (12 entries, one item each). If the orchestrator meant the block whose "batch" field equals 2 (653..604), this is the wrong block. Verdicts: 8 APPROVE (605, 608, 609, 611, 614, 617, 622, 627), 2 APPROVE-LINKOUT-ONLY (618, 623), 1 NEEDS-HUMAN-REVIEW (613), 1 REJECT (606). Rights tiers: A1 for 605, 608, 609, 611, 622, 627; A2 for 613, 614, 617, 618; C for 606 and 623. Every entry was fetched or read at least in part except 613 (host answers every request, robots.txt included, with a "Security Check / you're not a bot" page; not circumvented; identity taken from the Digital Commonwealth harvest of the same item) and 611's listed Perseus URL (robots Disallow, not fetched; the same article was read in the Internet Archive scan of SHSP vol. 24). Method: honest UA via tools/sources-qc/lib/http.mjs PoliteClient wrapper, cache first, per-host gaps persisted across processes (at least 1.3 s; hd.housedivided.dickinson.edu has Crawl-delay 600 in robots.txt, so only 5 uncached requests were made there, each 10 minutes apart); no browser launched; nothing under legacy/, tools/t0, tests/t0, ops, baseline, release, src/lib/time, tools/time or tools/data touched; no repository file written (scratch work in the session scratchpad, new cache entries only under tmp/sources-v2/cache). Not verified: anything on nytimes.com (robots.txt names anthropic-ai and ClaudeBot as disallowed; not fetched), chroniclingamerica.loc.gov (Cloudflare challenge page, not fetched past it), the Perseus page, Shreve's biography, the UI and OPenn manuscripts beyond the pages named.
systemic_findings: Batch indexing: queue file has batches[0..8] with a 1-based 'batch' field; I used the 0-based array index 2 (batch field 3: 605, 606, 608, 609, 611, 613, 614, 617, 618, 622, 623, 627). The task text 'batch number 2' is ambiguous; if the block with batch field 2 was wanted, this run covered the wrong 12.

House Divided (hd.housedivided.dickinson.edu) declares Crawl-delay: 600 in robots.txt; honouring it costs 10 minutes per uncached request, so only 5 uncached requests were made there. Future QC should lean on the probe cache (all 2018 blog PDFs are on housedivided.dickinson.edu, which has no robots.txt) and plan for one request per ten minutes on hd.*.

The registry probe misclassified entry 613: credo.library.umass.edu returns HTTP 200 with a 'Security Check / Just a moment' page for every URL including robots.txt, yet link_class says 'redirected'. It should be blocked_to_bots. chroniclingamerica.loc.gov also answers with a Cloudflare challenge (403) and the Wayback copy of the Credo page is the same challenge.

The registry probe cached only the first 327,680 bytes of the Donavin PDF (entry 623), which cannot be parsed; the full file is 14.3 MB and image-only (no text layer). Probe-cached large PDFs should be treated as unreadable unless 'truncated' is false.

Several list titles are the link text of the source blog post (Blog Divided, 'Beyond Gettysburg: Primary Sources for the Gettysburg Campaign', 11 June 2018), not the works' titles: 606 'Richard Southeron Shreve account' is a Google Books search hit in a 2002 book; 613 'Anonymous letter from a Cumberland County resident' is 'Letter from unidentified correspondent to Sidney Boden, 11 July 1863'; 623 'Rebel Occupation of Carlisle' is S. K. Donavin, 'The Invasion: Rebel Occupancy of Carlisle, 1863' (1998 journal reprint); 609 is a book, not a 'memoir'. Registry titles for these should be corrected before any use.

House Divided hosts transcriptions that are not exactly verbatim (entry 614: '[illegible]' where the scan reads 'residue', 'defense' for the scan's 'defence') and none of the House Divided pages read (record pages, About) states reuse terms; where House Divided is the only text source treat tier as A2 and prefer our own transcription from the scan.

For 3 of the 12 entries the better citation and text source is the Internet Archive: SHSP vol. 24 (southernhistoric24sout) for 611, Lockwood (ourcampaignaroun00lock, also Gutenberg #31258) for 609, Hoke (greatinvasionof100hoke) for 622, Kittochtinny vol. 4 (papersreadbefore04kitt) for 627. The Internet Archive 'date' field is the series start for multi-volume sets (1876 for SHSP, 1899 for Kittochtinny); title pages give 1896 and 1908.

The Historian value of this batch is small: 8 of 12 describe Carlisle or Chambersburg during the invasion, none describes the fighting at Gettysburg except Schuricht (611) and the compiled Hoke (622). 605, 614, 617 and 623 all concern the same night (the shelling of Carlisle, 1 July); 605 is by a gunner of Landis' battery (entries 595/599).

Policy notes for the owner: nytimes.com was not fetched because its robots.txt names anthropic-ai and ClaudeBot; the Perseus links stay unusable; no browser was launched; no files under the owned repository paths were written beyond the polite client's cache entries in tmp/sources-v2/cache.

items.written: Events of 24 June to 2 July 1863; OPenn dates the journal 1862-1863; the July 1 entry (fols. 59v-62r) was written up after the event ('I afterwards ascertained'), exact writing date unknown
items.rights_basis: Unpublished 1860s manuscript by Charles Ashmead Schaeffer (OPenn and PACSCL blog give 1843-1898), so the life+70 term has long ended. The holding repository (Krauth Memorial Library Archives, Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia) states twice, on the OPenn page and in the TEI file <licence> elements, that the metadata and 'these images and the content' are 'free of known copyright restrictions and in the public domain' under the Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0. No transcription exists, so any text is our own work. A counsel glance is still sensible because the basis is the repository's dedication plus author death, not an imprint year.
items.evidence: Fetched http://openn.library.upenn.edu/Data/0010/html/00_J91_42_P4529j.html (301/308 to https, HTTP 200, 190,738 B) and the TEI XML (73,263 B). Page title 'Journal of Charles Ashmead Schaeffer', call no. *00 J91.42 P4529j, 'Krauth Memorial Library Archives' (Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia, hosted by Penn's OPenn), date 'From 1862 to 1863'; summary says 'military combat in Carlisle, Pennsylvania'. The listed fragment #a60r exists (anchor in the HTML, table of contents 'fol. 60r - July 1, 1863'). Downloaded and read the web JPGs for fols. 59v, 60r, 60v, 61v, 62r (1028_0119, 0120, 0121, 0123, 0124). Fol. 59v: after joining Capt. Landis' artillery company he mustered, reached Harrisburg, was at Fort Washington until 1 July. Fol. 60r (dated July 1): marched toward Carlisle, reached it about 6 P.M., fed at the market house, about 7 P.M. heard the cry that the rebels were coming. Fol. 60v: shells fell in the square, his gun fired, Cpl. Patterson's fingers were struck. Fol. 61v-62r: firing ended about 11:30 P.M.; a man named Colladay died after amputation; at 3 A.M. three more shells; rebels reported gone; a hindsight sentence says they numbered 6,000-7,000 against 2,100. Two concrete description claims checked: (a) digitized manuscript diary: yes (185 image files, no text); (b) Union volunteer during the emergency: yes, Landis' battery (= entries 595/599). Independent corroboration of identity: Wikipedia via search result says Schaeffer served in the 'First Pennsylvania Battery' and was University of Iowa president 1887-98 (secondary, not fetched by me).
items.extraction_notes: Image-only handwriting (OPenn offers TIFF masters and 140-340 KB web JPGs; legible 19th-century hand); the OPenn TEI and the PACSCL blog page carry no transcription. Adapter manual-transcription; second person must check. Relevant text is about 6 manuscript pages, roughly 1,100-1,300 words, fols. 59v-62r (the June 18 and June 25 entries on 58v-59v are earlier context); OPenn's 'July 1' section begins at fol. 60r but the narrative that leads into it starts on 59v. Cite as C. A. Schaeffer, Journal, Krauth Memorial Library Archives call no. *00 J91.42 P4529j, fol. 59v-62r, via OPenn. Segment by day heading and folio, flag that the July 1 account is written with hindsight.
issues: Title says 'University of Pennsylvania OPenn': OPenn is only the hosting platform; the diary is held by the Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia (Krauth Memorial Library Archives). Author's full name is Charles Ashmead Schaeffer.
The entry reads as Carlisle context, not Gettysburg: the shelling of Carlisle on the night of 1/2 July is a separate action (Landis' battery, Gen. W. F. Smith's militia against Fitz Lee).
Not contemporaneous in the strict sense: at least the July 1 entry is a later write-up (text says 'afterwards ascertained').
Page is plain http in the list; fragment anchors work only on the https page.
Only fols. 59v-62r were read; the rest of the 90-folio journal (Boston Treasury chemistry work, 1862-63) was not.

items.evidence: Fetched http://hd.housedivided.dickinson.edu/node/36518 (301 to https, HTTP 200, cached 35,617 B): title 'New York Times, "A Word to Pennsylvania," June 26, 1863', citation 'New York Times, June 26, 1863, p. 4: 4', 'Newspaper: Headline A Word to Pennsylvania', 'Transcription not yet available'. Downloaded the page image it links (1863_06_26_pennsylvania.jpg, 574,458 B, sha256 fe0b1a68...; one request, honouring the host's Crawl-delay 600) and read it: a two-column clipping headed 'A Word to Pennsylvania'. Claims checked: (a) editorial criticising Pennsylvanians: 'We are amazed at the apathy that seems to prevail among the people of Pennsylvania' and it ends calling on Pennsylvanians 'to wake up, arm, organize'; (b) about the invasion in progress: 'It is now a fortnight since the rebels began their operations in Pennsylvania' (Jenkins reached Chambersburg 15 June) and 'our Harrisburg correspondent of this morning'. These internal marks fit 26 June 1863. The clipping has no masthead or date, so the date rests on House Divided's citation. nytimes.com was not fetched: its robots.txt has explicit Disallow groups for anthropic-ai and ClaudeBot.

Rome & Brothers ... 1864' read from the title page in the Internet Archive OCR of the NYPL scan (ourcampaignaroun00lock; IA metadata possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT, date 1864). Project Gutenberg #31258 (IA mirror ourcampaignaroun31258gut) is a proofed text of the same title page and its IA rights field says 'Public domain in the USA'; Gutenberg's own licence wording would apply to that file, so prefer the IA OCR or strip the licence.
items.evidence: Google Books bare page (cached) for id TdA_AAAAYAAJ: 'Our Campaign Around Gettysburg ... Twenty-third Regiment (N.Y.S.N.G.)', John Lockwood, A. H. Rome, 1864, Harvard copy, 168 pages, full view. Internet Archive metadata for ourcampaignaroun00lock (fetched): NYPL scan, 'Brooklyn : A. H. Rome', 1864, 186 images, djvu text 262,636 B (fetched and read). Title page text: 'Our Campaign Around Gettysburg: A Memorial of what was Endured, Suffered and Accomplished by the Twenty-third Regiment (N.Y.S.N.G.) and other regiments associated with them, in their Pennsylvania and Maryland campaign ... June-July, 1863 ... Brooklyn: A. H. Rome & Brothers ... 1864'. The preface says the author was 'connected with the Twenty-Third only during its absence' and speaks of 'my company', so he marched in the ranks as a militiaman. Narrative opens 'Off to the war ... Monday, June 15th', has a 1 July entry, an account of Fitz Hugh Lee's shelling of Carlisle seen from the march (p. 62, 'W. F. Smith then holding Carlisle'), a 'Sunday, July 5th' entry, and an appendix with the 23rd's own journal ('Tuesday, June 16th, 1863 - 23d Reg. received marching orders'). Gutenberg #31258 text (244,826 B) shows the same title page and credits the IA/American Libraries scan.
items.extraction_notes: Use archive-fulltext on ourcampaignaroun00lock_djvu.txt (OCR clean in the body, noisy in front matter) or the Gutenberg text; segment by dated entries and chapters; the appendix journal is the regiment's official record in another voice, attribute it separately. About 168 printed pages. Cite with printed page numbers (page_numbers.json exists for the IA item). Author name is not on the title page.
issues: The author's name John Lockwood (1825 or 6-1901) comes from library catalogues (NYPL via IA, Google Books, Gutenberg), not from the title page, which has none.
Title labels him '23rd NYSNG'; the preface says he was only attached to the regiment during the emergency.
Written up after the campaign for publication (1864): retrospective, not a diary.

Located the article in the Internet Archive scans: https://archive.org/details/southernhistoric24sout (metadata fetched: volume 24, Allen County Public Library, 408 images; djvu text 1,091,928 B read). The volume's index lists 'Schuricht, Diary of Lieutenant H.; Gettysburg Campaign, 339'. Article header: 'Jenkins' Brigade in the Gettysburg Campaign. Extracts from the Diary of Lieutenant Hermann Schuricht, of the Fourteenth Virginia Cavalry', reprinted 'From the Richmond Dispatch, April 5, 1896'; the introductory letter is dated 'Idlewild (near) Cobham, Va., April 1, 1896' and signed 'First Lieutenant of Company D, 14th Virginia Cavalry', and says he sends 'a translation from my diary' kept in German from 15 June to 14 July 1863. Claims checked: (a) Confederate cavalry officer in Jenkins' brigade: yes, he writes of 'General Jenkins' Cavalry Brigade', the 15 June entry covers Williamsport, Greencastle and Chambersburg, 27 June 'The entire brigade moved on to Carlisle'; (b) printed in SHSP: yes, vol. 24, pp. 339-350; later entries describe the approach to Gettysburg, the days of the battle and the retreat to Williamsport, ending 14 July. The same scan also carries 'A War Letter' (Richmond Enquirer correspondent, Jenkins' Brigade near Harrisburg, 30 June 1863) after the diary.
items.extraction_notes: Adapter archive-fulltext on southernhistoric24sout_djvu.txt (article at about OCR lines 17,505-18,050; pages 339-350). OCR noise is moderate (e.g. 'i86j' for 1863, 'ami' for 'and'); verify quotes against the page images. Segment by diary date. Stop the Schuricht text at the 14 July entry on p. 350: the following 'A War Letter' is another author's contemporary newspaper letter and must not be attributed to Schuricht. Text is a translation from German of unknown fidelity, published 33 years after the events (the editor's intro letter is 1896). Perseus must not be used.
issues: Listed Perseus link is robots-disallowed; replacement is the Internet Archive scan.
Author spelled Herman in the list; the article prints Hermann; he was a first lieutenant of Company D.
'Contemporaneous' needs a caveat: a 1863 diary, but we only have a 1896 English translation prepared for the press.
IA 'date' field says 1876 (series start); the correct imprint is 1896.

items.written: 1863-07-11 (Digital Commonwealth record of the same item; letter, 4 p.)
items.rights_basis: Unpublished anonymous 1863 letter, so almost certainly public domain, but the repository states 'Requests to publish, redistribute, or replicate this material should be addressed to Special Collections and University Archives, University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries' and 'license: Contact host institution for more information' (Digital Commonwealth harvest). Treat as link-out until UMass answers.
items.evidence: The listed URL answers HTTP 200 with a page titled 'Security Check / Just a moment... To confirm you're not a bot', for the page itself, for the host's robots.txt, and for the Wayback capture of 12 May 2026; I did not try to get past it. Identity was established elsewhere: Digital Commonwealth (robots allow search.json, Crawl-delay 5 honoured) harvested the UMass record whose identifier_local_other is mums605-s02-b006-i009: 'Letter from unidentified correspondent to Sidney Boden', date 11 July 1863, 4 p., Burgett-Irey Family Papers (MS 605), Series 2 Correspondence, subject Civil War. Its abstract: mail service had been suspended, rebel forces moved into the area without any resistance, the writer was faced with armed men at the door who asked if any abolitionists were around, cavalry and infantry filled the roads, 'Marion Weakley visited the area a day or two after they left Carlisle'. The UMass finding aid (fetched) says only 'a letter written by an unknown author' notes 'rebel forces occupying and plundering homes'. The record does not name where it was written; 'Cumberland County resident' is the list's (Blog Divided's) inference, unconfirmed. The letter text itself was not read.
items.extraction_notes: None possible by program: image-only manuscript behind a bot wall, repository permission required. A human should open the link once in a browser, read where it was written and who the writer is, and confirm the Credo image is viewable; then keep as link-out.
issues: Could not read the document: host serves a bot challenge for every request, including robots.txt (and the registry probe recorded it as 'redirected (HTTP 200)', which hides this).

Listed title 'Anonymous letter from a Cumberland County resident' is not what the repository calls it: 'Letter from unidentified correspondent to Sidney Boden', 11 July 1863; place of writing not stated in the record.
Part of the Burgett-Irey family papers (an Illinois family), whose connection to Cumberland County is unverified.
UMass reserves publication and replication; no licence.

items.written: 1863-07-10 (Carlisle Herald, p. 2 col. 5, per House Divided citation); reports the night of Wednesday 1 July
items.rights_basis: Underlying text is an 1863 local newspaper item (pre-1931 imprint) but the clipping image has no masthead or date, so date and page rest on House Divided's citation, and the only text is House Divided's own transcription ('Transcriber Don Sailer, Dickinson College, 05/03/2011'), whose reuse terms I could not find (no rights statement on the three House Divided pages read). It also deviates slightly from the scan. Prefer our own transcription from the image after a human confirms the host's terms.
items.evidence: Fetched http://hd.housedivided.dickinson.edu/node/33707 (301 to https, HTTP 200, cached): 'Carlisle (PA) Herald, "Behavior of Our Citizens Under Rebel Fire," July 10, 1863', citation p. 2, column 5, 'Date Certainty Exact', a full transcription (about 300 words, one paragraph) 'presented here in complete form ... Spelling and typographical errors have been preserved'. Downloaded and read the linked scan 1863_07_10_citzens.jpg (261,422 B, sha256 105fde9a...). Compared: the scan reads 'BEHAVIOR OF OUR CITIZENS UNDER REBEL FIRE.-When on Wednesday night of last week the chivalrous and soldierly Fitz Hugh Lee opened his batteries upon our women and children...' and gives Gen. Smith about three thousand militia, a militia battery and one company of regular cavalry, matching the transcription. Two deviations: scan has 'residue' where the transcription has '[illegible]', and 'defence' where the transcription prints 'defense'. Description claim 'local newspaper account of Carlisle residents during the shelling': yes, it credits citizens of Capt. Kuhn's, Low's and Black's companies with a skirmish line at Letort spring. 'Wednesday night of last week' is 1 July 1863, consistent with an issue of 8-10 July.
items.extraction_notes: One paragraph, about 300 words, one passage. Take the text from the scan, not the House Divided transcription, or correct the transcription against the image before use. Cite as Carlisle (Pa.) Herald, 10 July 1863, p. 2, col. 5. Partisan tone ('dastardly dog') needs a Unionist-newspaper label.
issues: House Divided's transcription is not exactly verbatim: '[illegible]' for a legible word and a spelling change.
Clipping has no date line; the date and column come from the host's citation.
Page is plain http in the list.
House Divided's reuse terms not found.

items.rights_basis: Unpublished private letter of 1863 by Hanna Culver, a sister of Joseph F. Culver (born 1834), so by any plausible dates her life+70 term has ended and it is public domain on the author-death basis, but I did not find her dates. The text on the list is a House Divided transcription (with '[?]' guesses and an editor's caption) of a letter held by the University of Iowa Libraries; neither host's reuse terms were found.
items.evidence: Fetched the PDF at the listed URL (301 to https, HTTP 200, cached 49,732 B, 2 pages, sha256 bd2c3776...) and extracted the text layer. Caption: 'Hanna Culver from Carlisle to her brother Joseph F. Culver, Joseph Franklin Culver collection, Special Collection, University of Iowa library. Her brother was serving with the 129th Illinois Infantry in Tennessee.' Letter: 'East Villa July 9th /63 Dear Brother'. Claims checked: (a) occupation: Jenkins entered about eleven on Saturday (27 June), Ewell's main body arrived at three, Ewell's corps left on Tuesday morning along the Baltimore pike, citizens' stores sacked; (b) shelling: Smith's brigade arrived about seven on Wednesday evening, 'Stuarts gorillas under command of Fitzhugh Lee' threw shells, a flag of truce was refused, a general cannonade lasted about four hours, gasworks and garrison burned, 'Seventeen of our Soldiers were wounded two of whom had a limb amputated'. It also reports 'Gen. Lee has been so badly beaten at Gettiesburg', and that relatives had gone to see the battleground. Family context cross-checked on the University of Iowa blog for entry 618: the father Joseph Culver (72) lived in Carlisle's East Ward. The Blog Divided category page (fetched) lists this PDF as 'Culver Family Correspondence - Hanna Culver's July 9, 1863 letter detailing the occupation and shelling'.
items.extraction_notes: Adapter pdf-text: the PDF has a good text layer, about 6,500 characters, 8 paragraphs. Do not quote the two-line House Divided caption as Hanna's words. Transcriber's '[?]' marks (e.g. '[late?]', '[town?]', '[Burg?]') mean uncertain readings; check every quote against the Iowa manuscript images (not located by me) before shipping. Cite as Hanna Culver to Joseph F. Culver, 9 July 1863, Joseph Franklin Culver Collection, University of Iowa Special Collections, via House Divided transcription.
issues: Rights: host transcription of a manuscript held by Iowa; terms not found for either.
Transcription is the host's, with uncertain readings and no page images attached to it.
Spelling Hanna vs Hannah (the Iowa blog writes 'sister Hannah').
Mixes occupation and the post-battle news, but nothing from inside the Gettysburg battle.

items.rights_basis: Letter of Joseph F. Culver (born 3 Nov 1834, died 20 Jan 1899 per the site's introduction), so the 1863 text is public domain by author death. But the web page is a University of Iowa Libraries web edition of a published book of the letters (edited by Leslie W. Dunlap, with explanatory notes by Edwin C. Bearss): the text has editor-added punctuation and paragraphing and carries the notes in double parentheses. Those layers are copyrightable and no licence is stated on the pages read.
items.evidence: Fetched https://blog.lib.uiowa.edu/culver/1863/6-27b/ (HTTP 200, 42,884 B; cached). Header 'Head Quarters, Co. "A", 129th Ills. Gallatin, Tenn., June 27th 1863 Dear Mary', signed 'J. F.'. Claim checked: 'Union soldier's letter expressing concern for his father in Carlisle': the letter says he sees by the papers that Carlisle is in possession of the rebels and 'I greatly fear the shock will be too great for Father to bear'; note says the father Joseph Culver was 72 and lived in Carlisle's East Ward. The rest is domestic (lost trunks, Sunday school, Mary's travel to New York). Fetched the site's About and Introduction pages: the site republishes letters 150 years to the day, 'Your Affectionate Husband, J.F. Culver: Letters Written During the Civil War' is the book, J. F. Culver was first lieutenant then captain of Company A, 129th Illinois, born near Carlisle. No licence or copyright statement appears on the three pages.
items.extraction_notes: Do not ingest from the web page: text is an edited transcription with editorial punctuation, and the double-parenthesis notes are not Culver's words. If ever used, strip ((...)) notes and bracketed insertions and check against the manuscript images in the Iowa collection. Only the first sentence bears on the invasion (about 40 words).
issues: The letter is written in Tennessee: no first-hand knowledge of Carlisle; value is only news reception on 27 June.
Title 'Joseph Culver letter' can be confused with the 72-year-old father Joseph Culver; the writer is his son Joseph F. Culver.
Two June 27 posts exist on the site; the listed one (6-27b) is the one that mentions Carlisle.
Web text is a modern edition with editorial additions.

items.written: Published 1887 (Dayton, Ohio: W. J. Shuey); events 15 June to July 1863
items.rights_basis: Original imprint 'Dayton, Ohio: W. J. Shuey, Publisher. 1887. Copyright, 1887, by W. J. Shuey' read from the title page in the Internet Archive OCR of the NYPL scan (greatinvasionof100hoke; IA metadata date 1887, possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT). IA also lists a 1959 item (bwb_Y0-BDN-722) and Google-scanned copies: exclude reprints.
items.evidence: Google Books bare page (cached) for JbMTAAAAYAAJ: 'The Great Invasion of 1863: Or, General Lee in Pennsylvania ... Jacob Hoke, W. J. Shuey, 1887, original from NYPL, 613 pages'. Internet Archive: greatinvasionof100hoke (NYPL scan, 644 images; metadata fetched), djvu text 1,306,574 B read. Title page: 'Embracing an account of the strength and organization of the armies of the Potomac and Northern Virginia; their daily marches ...; the three days of battle; the retreat ... with an appendix containing an account of the burning of Chambersburg'. The listed anchor pg=PA97 matches printed p. 97: it is Hoke's own narrative of Monday 15 June, citizens and 'colored persons' fleeing Chambersburg ('we witnessed the greatest excitement'). Claim 'includes the seizure of Black residents': yes, printed pp. 107-109 'Capture of Negroes': cavalrymen rode into wheat fields after them, 'In two cases ... I succeeded in effecting the release of the captured persons', and it quotes Rev. Dr. Schaff's diary on free-born persons sent south. The preface says he 'drew largely' on other writers' published articles, so only part is his own eyewitness narrative; an author's note in the text says he was a member of J. Hoke & Co., merchants, Chambersburg (certificate quoted in the text). The entry's 'book-length account by a Chambersburg merchant who witnessed the invasion' is therefore true for chapters on Chambersburg but understates the book: it is a compiled 600-page history of the whole campaign and the three days of battle.
items.extraction_notes: Adapter archive-fulltext on greatinvasionof100hoke_djvu.txt with printed-page citations (page_numbers.json is present). OCR is noisy ('Dee' for Lee, 'Dongstreet', 'Dieutenant'). Segment by chapter; Chapters III-IV (from printed p. 89) are the Chambersburg narrative; much of the book quotes other authors (Early, Longstreet, Schaff, battlefield eyewitnesses), which must be attributed to the quoted author, not to Hoke. Already in the Historian's catalogue (registry catalog_overlap H2:SRC-23); check for duplication before ingesting.
issues: Description understates scope: the book is a compilation covering the whole campaign, battle and retreat, not only Chambersburg.
Retrospective (1887) with an editorial point of view ('wrote from the standpoint of a Unionist'), much of it second-hand.
Google Books anchor pg=PA97 not requestable; confirmed against the IA OCR printed page 97.
Beware the 1959 reprint and other modern editions on IA.

items.written: Original account printed 9 July 1863 (Carlisle American Volunteer; also Herald 10 July and American 15 July); this PDF is Cumberland County History vol. 15 no. 1 (Summer 1998), pp. 34-50
items.rights_basis: The linked file is a 1998 edited reprint in a journal of the Cumberland County Historical Society (the society's Gardner Library site states 'Copyright 2014-2026 Cumberland County Historical Society All rights reserved'); the editor corrected spelling, punctuation and Ewell's name and added photographs credited to the Society. The 1863 newspaper text is public domain, but this scan is not that text. The PDF is image-only.
items.evidence: Fetched the listed PDF in full with a range request (the registry's cached copy was cut at 327,680 B and cannot be parsed): 14,277,065 B, 17 pages, no text layer, sha256 ae5f17ca.... I rendered and read pages 1, 2, 3, 5, 15, 16 and 17. Page 1: 'The Invasion: Rebel Occupancy of Carlisle, 1863. S.K. Donavin' with an editor's note: the account 'was printed in the Carlisle American Volunteer on July 9, 1863, in the Carlisle Herald ... July 10, and in the Carlisle American on July 15'; it is 'reprinted here from the American Volunteer, with only a few changes and corrections in spelling and punctuation' and 'General Ewell's name ... has been as consistently corrected'. Journal page numbers run 34-50. Section headings (The First Alarm, The Entrance of the Rebels, The Burning of the Barracks, Third Shelling Commenced); journal p. 49 says 'Some eighteen of the soldiers were wounded but none killed' and then adds other American Volunteer items (Milroy's wagon train; 18 June 'The Rebel Raid in Our Valley'). Fetched https://gardnerlibrary.org/journal/invasion-rebel-occupancy-carlisle-1863 (HTTP 200, Crawl-delay 10 honoured): same article, 'Journal Issue 1998 Summer, Volume 15, Issue 1', author Donavin, S. K., with the same editor's note.
items.extraction_notes: Not extractable (scanned images, modern edition). If the Historian wants this account it should come from the 1863 newspaper itself (Carlisle American Volunteer, 9 July 1863) from an open scan; I tried chroniclingamerica.loc.gov and it answered with a Cloudflare challenge, so I did not pursue it. Cite as S. K. Donavin, 'The Invasion: Rebel Occupancy of Carlisle, 1863', Cumberland County History 15:1 (1998) 34-50.
issues: Entry title 'Rebel Occupation of Carlisle (Carlisle newspaper account)' hides that the file is a 1998 journal reprint with editorial changes.
Author S. K. Donavin (Simpson K. Donavin, per the editor) is not named in the list.
PDF contains more than the Donavin account (other June 1863 American Volunteer items, photographs, editor's notes).
Registry probe cached only the first 327,680 bytes of the PDF.

items.written: Letter written Monday evening 15 June to Thursday 18 June 1863; read before the Society 29 March 1906; printed 1908
items.rights_basis: Original imprint: volume title page 'Papers read before the Society from March, 1905 to February, 1908 ... Chambersburg, Pa., Repository Printing Rooms, 1908' (OCR shows 'J908'; the dated contents up to April 1908 fit). Any plausible reading is before 1931. IA metadata date field says 1899, the series start; it must not be used.
items.evidence: Internet Archive item papersreadbefore04kitt (metadata fetched: volume 4, Allen County Public Library Genealogy Center, 728 images, date field '1899'; djvu text 852,121 B read). Contents list: 'Jenkins Raid, By Mrs. Jermima K, Cree ... 92'. Text (printed pp. 92-99): 'The following paper written by Mrs. Jemima K. Cree to her absent husband, John Cree, in Pittsburg, gives a graphic account of the stirring scenes and incidents during the Jenkins raid in Chambersburg, June 15-19, 1863, and was also read at the meeting March 29, 1906.' Letter headed 'Monday evening, June 15, 1863. My dear Husband'. Claim checked: 'failed attempt to free her free-born servant': she writes Jenkins' men were 'gathering up our Darkies', and that 'I interceded for Mag, told them she was free born, etc. The man said he could do nothing'; Mag and Fannie were marched away; the word 'servant' is the list's inference but fits (they are 'our' household help, Mag's clothes and child were at the Cree relatives' house). Other checks: dated sections Monday 15 June, Tuesday evening, Tuesday morning, Thursday morning.
items.extraction_notes: Adapter archive-fulltext on papersreadbefore04kitt_djvu.txt (paper at about OCR lines 4,340-4,660, about 2,900 words, printed pp. 92-99); OCR slips ('tie General', 'ami boys'); segment by date headings and paragraph. Cite as Jemima K. Cree to John Cree, 15-18 June 1863, in Papers Read Before the Kittochtinny Historical Society, vol. 4 (1908), pp. 92-99. Note the 1906 reading was of a private letter edited for print.
issues: Entry date '1908' is the printing year; the letter is 15-18 June 1863 and was read before the Society in 1906.
IA date field '1899' is the series start, not the volume's date.
'Servant' is an inference; the text says 'our Darkies' and names Mag and Fannie.
Jenkins raid is pre-battle (15-17 June); nothing on Gettysburg.
